history.period: 1660 CE; original wooden structure destroyed by fire in 1905, rebuilt in stone/concrete
history.summary: The chief temple of the Kullu valley, at Sultanpur near the Rupi Palace. Built in 1660 CE by Raja Jagat Singh to atone for the sin of killing a brahmin (local narrative: his food turned to worms). The Rama-Sita idol was brought from Ayodhya, and Jagat Singh declared himself and his heirs chharibardar (custodians) of Raghunath rather than kings - a status the Kullu royal family asserts to this day, calling themselves mere viceroys of the deity. The Kullu Dussehra festival (one account dates it to 1651) centres on Raghunathji. The 1905 fire destroyed the original wooden structure; the temple was rebuilt in stone and concrete. Ownership has been disputed: in 2016 the Kullu royal family's Maheshwar Singh accused the state government of taking over the temple after cash-and-idol thefts in 2014 - current status (verify). Architecture blends Pahari and Pyramidal styles with a shikhara.

name: Raghunath Temple
town: Sultanpur (Kullu town; CSV town 'Kullu' is approximate)
town_description: Kullu is the main town of the Kullu Valley on the Beas River, known as Kuluta in antiquity and called the 'Valley of Gods' for its hundreds of temples. It was the capital of the Kullu kingdom under rulers like Jagat Singh, and today is famous for the week-long Kullu Dussehra festival and as a commercial base for travellers heading to Manali and the Parvati Valley. Sultanpur, where the temple stands behind the Rupi Palace, is the old core of the town.

travel.airport: Bhuntar airport, ~10-12 km from Kullu town (verify)
travel.road: ~1 km from Dhalpur (Kullu bus stand), behind the Rupi Palace; easily reached on foot

visitor_information.opening_hours: Morning aarti ~7 AM (summer)/8 AM (winter); closed 11:30 AM-5:30 PM (summer) and 12:30-4 PM (winter), per a visitor review (verify)
